title: Coming from another language — the Vyrn guide

chapter.title: Coming from another language
chapter.lede: What carries over from Rust, TypeScript or Go, what is deliberately different, and what Vyrn does not have at all.

sections.heading: Validation
prose: The thing that is most likely to be new is where a rule lives. In the languages beside it a rule is code somebody has to call: a constructor, a schema object, a validating function. The type says nothing about whether it ever ran. In Vyrn the rule is part of the type, so Age is a number that has passed it.

The compiler proves what it can while the program compiles. So Age(30) costs nothing at run time, and Age(5) is a compile error rather than a failed check. Input from outside the program is not a constant, so it takes the total form. Age?(n) answers Option<Age>, and no path produces an unchecked Age.

sections.heading: Ownership
prose: Rust says this with borrows and lifetimes, TypeScript cannot say it at all, and Go says it with a pointer and a comment. Vyrn writes the intent on the parameter as a word: read, modify, consume.

There is no lifetime grammar to learn, because the word is the whole declaration — the compiler decides where the value is released from what the words say. Ownership, consume, regions is the chapter that teaches it.

sections.heading: Errors
prose: There is no null and no exception. An absent value is Option, a failure is Result, and ? hands a failure to the caller unchanged — the same three shapes Rust uses, without the conversion traits.
A panic is for a case that cannot happen. Nothing unwinds: there is no catch anywhere in the language, so a panic ends the program.

sections.heading: Records and enums
prose: A record is a struct with named fields and no inheritance. An enum is a closed choice with payloads, and match covers every case. The compiler counts the arms, so a new variant is a compile error at every site that reads it.

Generics are monomorphised, protocols are how a type says what it can do, and a protocol bound is checked at the call rather than at run time. Records are structural, as in TypeScript: a record with the same fields, or more, fits where a record type is wanted.

sections.heading: What Vyrn does not have
prose: No garbage collector. Memory is released where the ownership words say it is, and the editor's hover shows that decision per binding.
No exceptions, no unwinding, no async colour. A program is a program; the runtime that serves HTTP is a library written in the language.
No macros. A generator is an ordinary Vyrn function that runs while you compile and emits Vyrn — vyrn emit-gen prints exactly what it wrote. gen fns and generators is the chapter.
No inheritance and no null. Both are covered above, and neither has a workaround to learn.

sections.heading: Next steps
prose: If you write Rust: read Ownership first — it is the chapter where this language differs from yours the most, and it is shorter than you expect.
If you write TypeScript: read Values and types and then Errors. Numbers state their width here, and validation is a type rather than a library.
If you write Go: read Records, enums, match — the closed enum and exhaustive match are what replace the interface-and-type-switch pattern.
The benchmarks answer the other question a reader arrives with, and every reading there is published.
